Yes, the ROMs are different.  Here are some helpful articles about them:

1) Identifying the Bally/Astrocade On-Board ROM

2) SNEAK UP AND BITE YA DEPARTMENT

https://www.ballyalley.com/faqs/BIOS%20Comparison/astrocade_bios_comparison.txt

The story behind the different ROMS is:
I can't remember his name, but the main man in charge of Bally when they were manufacturing the arcade was playing Gunfight and at the time of the 1st ROM you could only score 99 wins before the game would stop counting.He got there and was not very happy that he couldn't score any more than that. He told production that they needed to make it 9999. So to do that they need to move all of the code after that point 5 bytes. Thus the '64 versus the '59 bios change was made. As far as the differences between the Whitey and the rest, was just a date change.

130 if TR(1)goto 150 140 goto 110 150 ....

About the Book:

From early classics like Contact to marvels like High Speed, gaming publisher Williams dazzled arcade goers with its diverse range of quality pinball games. The age of video games catapulted the company into legend with blockbusters like Defender and Joust, and by the end of the 1980s it was the largest coin-op publisher in North America. Williams’ acquisition of Bally/Midway began a period of hits that included Mortal Kombat and NBA Jam, as well as the best-selling pinball machine of all time, The Addams Family.

The history of Williams spans nearly six decades and is filled with great games, huge gambles and technical innovations that impacted every aspect of pinball and arcade video games. With interviews of 40+ former designers and executives from Williams/Bally/Midway, as well as information from hundreds of contemporaneous news reports and documents, this book presents a never-before-seen chronology of how the small company became a coin-op juggernaut. Thirty pinball and 26 video game classics are examined in depth with direct input from the people who made them, along with the story of the events that shaped one of gaming’s greatest publishing houses.

Anything I say will be oversimplifying, and it's not like I even understand it completely, but there are sort of two ways models like GPT learn. First, it trains on massive amounts of data, including scrapes of the web that may well include Bally Alley. Second, it has a context of an individual conversation, and will consider the prior messages back and forth when crafting its response. One of the big advances the last couple of years has been to massively increase the context length, so you give a big document to analyze or have a long, coherent conversation. There's still a limit, but it's much better than it used to be. So, my OpenAI account has the conversation about typing in programs where I explained the format and offered corrections. Now, rather than starting from scratch, I can go back to that conversation and give it new programs, and it already understands the basics about what to do.

Yes, you could, within reason, upload FAQs and such and it could answer questions about them. And as long as you keep the same conversation going, it will keep that in its working memory, at least until you run up against the context length limit.

I honestly do think there's knee-jerk aversion to change here. Creative types who wouldn't hesitate to use a machine to do manual labor suddenly balk once a machine can do the type of work they've specialized in. People who were skeptical of copyrights now want to expand copyright protection to elements like style and learning from sources.

The tools, as they exist today, are fun and make me a little more productive. On June 13, 2024, Ken Lill wrote, "What is the $ significance in lines 390 - 400? I have NEVER seen anything like that in Bally BASIC."

The $ command is only available in Bally BASIC.  It is used to access the Bally Arcade's on-board calculator routines.  I believe it is an undocumented command and is referenced in J. Fenton's 1979 document, called "Bally BASIC Hacker's Guide," where Fenton explains, somewhat, how to use the $ command.  You can read it here:

https://www.ballyalley.com/basic/bally_basic_hackers_guide.pdf

The $ command was removed from AstroBASIC.  Fenton mentions this in the document called "New and Improved BALLY BASIC" (called "Differences Between Bally and AstroBASIC" on BallyAlley.com).  Fenton wrote:

"Deleted Features - BCD MATH - The interface to 16 digit BCD math calculations ($ command) has been kicked out."

You can read about other Bally BASIC features that were added and removed from AstroBASIC, here:

https://www.ballyalley.com/basic/new_bally_basic.txt

I think that either the "Arcadian" or "Cursor" (possibly both) give short tutorials on how to use the $ command.  I don't blame Ken for overlooking this command, as it wasn't used often.  Since the expanded BASICs are built on Bally BASIC and not AstroBASIC, I'm trying to remember if Blue Ram BASIC and/or Vipersoft BASIC still have the $ command built into them.

I found something that saves a few bytes that a lot of people do when learning BASIC and how I would save a few precious bytes.


130 if TR(1)goto 150
140 goto 110
150 ....

I would use:
130 if TR(1)=0goto 110
150 ....

either way, you are in a loop until you pull the trigger #1 but you save:
2 bytes for the line number 1 byte for the goto
3 bytes for the 110 and 1 byte for the GO at the end of the line 140.
however, it did cost 2 bytes for the =0
end result is a savings of 5 bytes and less program

for the "gosub and goto" commands to go through after this area.
On a lengthy program these savings could speed up your game.

It does have one distinct advantage over the Bally Magic Functions processing. When utilizing magic functions, a machine language (ML) graphic subroutine is required. Unfortunately, the Z80 has to fetch each ML instruction from memory to execute the entire subroutine. These fetching cycles increase (delay) the total execution time of the entire subroutine.

The transfer board acts like a digital graphics subroutine. Outputting the last graphic parameter to the transfer board port 7EH initializes this digital subroutine, forcing the Z80 into a wait state. Once the subroutine is finished, the Z80 resumes executing. So even though the transfer board uses some slow CMOS gates, there are no "fetching" delays.

The custom Bally address/data chips were originally designed to be interfaced with DRAM, which had 6 A0-A5 pins used for both row and column addresses plus separate single data in and data output pins.

With static RAM, there is usually an 8 bit bidirectional data bus. For the Astrocade screen SRAM, the 6 SRAM pins A0-A5 are use for the row addresses. The 6 SRAM pins A6-A11 are used for the column addresses.

MCM Design's low/hi-res screen SRAM scheme is complex. Part of this scheme was taken from the Datamax UV-1R computer. I personally designed the single active low RAS, the row/column and the 8 bit data bus interfacing connected to the 4 hi-res SRAM banks plus some additional screen SRAM support schemes.

The entire low/hi-res SRAM scheme is detailed using five DWGS 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 plus an additional schematic for the auto low/hi-res select option.

HOW ARE THE CUSTOM ADDRESS RAS0, RAS1, RAS2 AND RAS3 LINES UTILIZED?

These 4 active high RAS lines are fed to a 74LS175 chip. The four Q outputs at this chip serve 2 purposes:
1. The four Q outputs are fed to a 4 gate combo acting like a 4 input NOR gate, which generates a single active low RAS line.
2. The four Q outputs are also fed to a second 74F175 chip. The four inverted Q outputs at this 74F175 chip generate the active low CAS0, CAS1, CAS2 and CAS3 lines, which are used as the 4 hi-res screen SRAM chip selects (CS).

HOW ARE THE SIX A0-A5 ROW AND COLUMN ADDRESSES FROM THE ASTROCADE MOTHERBOARD U20 OUTPUTS STROBED INTO EACH OF THE 4 SCREEN SRAM CHIPS?
1. When the 6 bit row address appears at the U20 outputs, the 6 outputs also appear at the six inputs of a 74F373 latching chip. This row address is latched to each of the 4 screen SRAM A0-A5 inputs, when that single active low RAS line "mentioned above" goes low.
2. When the 6 bit column address appears at the U20 outputs, the 6 outputs also appear at the A6-A11 screen SRAM inputs.

One of the SRAM chip selects CAS0 thru CAS3 will go low enabling the appropriate SRAM (hi-res bank) for a Z80 screen SRAM write or read.

Each of the screen SRAM chip's 8 bit data bus MD0-MD7 is wired to a separate bidirectional transceiver 74LS245.

The appropriate hi-res bank transceiver is enabled using a bank select scheme centered around a 74F138 selector.
The Z80 memory address lines A1 and A0, used for a Z80 screen SRAM hi-res bank write or read, also help select the appropriate hi-res bank, where:
A1 A0 = selected bank
00 = Bank 0
01 = Bank 1
10 = Bank 2
11 = Bank 3

There is also an auto low/hi-res select scheme which determines automatically if just 1 bank/1 transceiver is utilized for low-res or if 4 banks/4 transceivers are utilized for hi-res operation.

The above screen SRAM operation description might make more sense if you could see the screen SRAM electronic schematics.

Unfortunately, because of the way the custom address/data chips scan (read) the 4 hi-res banks, there must be 4 SEPARATE hi-res banks. That's why four 74LS166  bit shifter chips are utilized for the hi-res TV display scan.

Back in 1981, Perkins Engineering modified a Bally motherboard for low/medium/hi-res operation. The modification was clever and messy. Wrapping wire was laying all over the top of the motherboard. Hi Mr Gorf. I have some additional info for you relating to the stars/sparkle colors (SSC) scheme.

Because I successfully bread boarded the SSC scheme on my hi-res Astrocade, I can tell you that the custom I/O chip's audio output line does NOT interact with the SSC scheme in any way.

If you look at the SSC scheme in the WOW operating manual, you will not see an audio line input to that scheme.

You will see the following inputs to the SSC scheme:
The Serial 1 and the Serial 0 pixel shifting lines output from the hi-res TV display scan (read) scheme,
the 4 stars, sparkle colors 01, 10 and 11 latched output lines from the WOW input port U6 MC14099 chip,
the vertical and horizontal drive outputs from the custom data chip,
the system inverted 7M clock
and finally the system active low Reset.

Somehow, the SSC scheme manipulates the video output line coming from the custom data chip.

In my bread boarded SSC scheme, I used the 74LS175 chip as the input port latch. I used the 4 inverted Q outputs for the 4 SSC input option latches, so that the SSC scheme would not interfere with the low-res graphics mode during a manual system reset. My hi-res Astrocade system reset will shut off all 4 of the SSC graphic options at one time.

The WOW SSC input port is set up differently. Reference the July 24, 2024 Discussion Group posting, message #21632.

The input port actually acts like an output port when the Z80 executes two instructions that have the form:

LD A,n1
IN(A),n2

Where n1 indicates which of the 4 SSC options are to be turned on or off.
The 4 SSC graphic options are:
twinkle stars (pixel color 00 = black for outer space)
sparkle pixel color 01
sparkle pixel color 10
sparkle pixel color 11

and where n2 = the input port number (hex#).

You can play around with the four U20 74LS257 video resistors to adjust the stars twinkling intensity. I only use 2 resistors for my hi-res Astrocade.

The composite video driver, required for the SSC scheme, must be compatible with the single SSC video output line.

If you are considering adding the SSC scheme to your upgraded Astrocade vision, you should probably breadboard the scheme to check for bugs.

Hi again Mr Gorf.

Attached are 4 photos that should give you a good idea how I bread boarded the WOW SSC scheme and interfaced it to my Ultimate Astrocade upper assembly.

I had to mount on the motherboard, a 14 pin machine tooled WW socket upside down and to the right of the Astrocade reset button.

Specific signal lines (#30 wrapping wires) were solder tapped from the motherboard bottom and wire wrapped to the 14 pin socket.

A short ribbon cable with 14 pin DIL ribbon cable connectors fed the signal lines to the breadboard, which was mounted upside down onto the low/hi-res screen SRAM Board 1.

I created a machine language (ML), hi-res graphic patterns test demo that could turn on or off any of the SSC scheme 4 graphic options by simply pressing the appropriate key on the Astrocade 24 button keypad. This ML program ran in the cartridge slot.

Initially, the 4 latch option lines were wired to the 4 normal 74LS175 Q outputs (pins 2, 7, 10 and 15). I saw the low-res menu go nuts with sparkling all over the TV display during a power on or with a system reset.

Later, I came up with the idea to wire the 4 latch lines to the inverted Q outputs (pins 3, 6, 11 and 14), so all the sparkling during the low-res mode would shut off.

The SSC scheme was intended for hi-res which scans (reads) hi-res screen RAM using the custom data chip Serial 0 and Serial 1 pixel shift input lines.

In low-res, the custom data lines MD0-MD7 are used to scan the low-res screen RAM for the TV display.

The SSC scheme would likely have to be modified or maybe redesigned for low-res operation, if that is possible. I don't have that expertise to investigate that possibility.

I also wanted to let you know that in a few months, I will schedule a 2nd attempt to generate a medium-res map. I have some new ideas that might increase the chance of successfully displaying a med-res map. I do have a hi-res Astrocade reason for spending more time with the med-res graphics mode.

Some time ago, I examined Perkins modified for hi-res motherboard interfacing schematic, which is archived on the Bally Alley. I documented my experiments with his med-res scheme and detailed the scheme's Theory Of Operation. An interest in the the med-res mode has recently emerged again. So, what it's worth to you guys, here is how Perkins around 1981 mapped a medium-res graphic mode on a Bally motherboard using the Bally custom Address/Data chips.

Perkins simulated the medium-res mode (160 x 204 pixels) by passing the Bally motherboard PX clock to the clock inhibit pin 15 in each of his four 74LS165 bit shift chips.

This would apparently shift the screen RAM bits (pixels) ONLY for the hi-res banks 0 and 1 into the two SERIAL 0 and SERIAL 1 custom Data chip input pins for the TV display, while inhibiting (turning off) the pixel shifting for banks 2 and 3.

The hi-res banks 2 and 3 were still accessable by the Z80, but were not mapped to the TV display.

Perkins used an inverted 7M clock for the hi-res TV display scanning scheme.

Because only banks 0 and 1 were utilized for the med-res mode, the screen RAM address byte mapping was unorthodox.

Perkins used a "mirrored" output port 08H keeping bit 0 for that port unchanged, where bit 0 defines: 0= low-res, 1= hi-res graphic mode). He also used bit 1 of the "mirrored" port as the med-res graphic mode bit. Setting bit 1=1 would request the hi-res mode to be modified to map the TV display in med-res.

By outputting 0000 0011 to port 08H, the custom Address/Data chips would operate in hi-res. However, with bit 1 also set to 1, additional logic gates decoded that set bit to pass the PX clock to the 4 hi-res pixel shift chips (74LS165) to INHIBIT pixel shifting of hi-res banks 2 and 3. Perkins med-res scheme was very clever and apparently worked.

Perkins med-res simulation scheme is so simplistic, we should be able to duplicate his work. I know I am going to make a second attempt, in a few months, to duplicate his work. I have some new ideas to try out.
